About the property

218 River Road sits a mile and a half north of the village of Rhinebeck, behind a half-mile of gravel drive that runs first through a row of old-growth sugar maples and then opens onto a clearing of roughly an acre. The house — a 1925 center-hall farmhouse on a fieldstone foundation — has been in three families across its first century, and in each of them somebody seems to have known when to leave it alone. The original wide-plank pine floors are intact in every room of the main level and most of the second. The sash windows still hold their original weights. The brass thumb-latches on the interior doors are the ones the carpenter installed, slightly loose now but working.

What has been done — and there has been work done, carefully — is the kind of thing that lets an old house keep functioning into another generation. The roof was redone in standing-seam copper in 2018. The kitchen was rebuilt in 2021 by a local cabinetmaker who matched the original wainscot detail in the pantry and chose soapstone for the counters on the theory that it would patinate the way the rest of the house has. A second-floor bath was added in 2019 in what had been a sewing room, with the plumbing run inside an unused chase so no wall opened up that didn't need to. The electric is on a 200-amp panel from 2017. The well was retested in February.

The land is the second thing the property is selling, and arguably the first. Eight and four-tenths acres run from the road back to a small spring-fed pond that the previous owner stocked with brook trout twenty years ago and has been quietly self-sustaining since. Between the house and the pond is a working orchard of nineteen apple trees — primarily heritage varieties: Newtown Pippin, Roxbury Russet, a few Esopus Spitzenburg the last owner started from scion — and three pear trees that the resident bear apparently ignores. The orchard is mowed but not maintained as commercial production; the new owner will inherit a freezer's worth of cider every fall whether they want it or not.

The barn — a single-bay dairy structure of roughly the same vintage as the house — was converted in 2020 into a studio and guest space. It has its own septic line, a wood stove, a kitchenette, a sleeping loft, and a writing desk built into the south wall under a triple steel window. It is the kind of building that solves a problem you didn't know you had, which is where to put the in-laws, where to write the novel, where to set up a printmaking press. It has been used, by the current owner, mostly to read in.

The house has good bones in the way that phrase is meant to be meant. The center-hall plan opens, on the right, into a formal living room with the original fireplace; on the left, into a long dining room that has hosted four weddings and a hundred Tuesday-night dinners. The kitchen runs across the back of the house with a south-facing pantry window and a back door that opens onto a flagstone terrace. Upstairs are four bedrooms, including a primary with a window seat overlooking the orchard, plus the new bath and the original. The third floor — a partially finished attic — is currently used as a reading room and could accommodate a fifth bedroom or a generous office without much structural conversation.

The village of Rhinebeck is twenty minutes on foot or four minutes by car, and the Rhinecliff Amtrak station — eighty minutes to Penn Station — is six minutes south. Bard College is a fifteen-minute drive north. The river itself — visible from the upstairs windows in the leafless months — is a short walk through the neighboring conservancy land. The property abuts a 60-acre easement parcel on its western boundary, which is what guarantees the pond view will not change in the lifetime of anyone reading this listing.

The current owner has lived here for nineteen years. Before that, the house belonged to a family who held it for forty-one. There is a measure-mark on the kitchen door frame for every child of both eras. They will stay with the house.

This is a property for someone who wants an old house that still feels like an old house — one that has been kept up without being scrubbed of its history, on a piece of land that allows for a small orchard, a real garden, and the kind of slow-moving daily life that the Hudson Valley quietly specializes in. We expect a careful round of showings; we are happy to walk it with you twice.

The house has been kept up without being scrubbed of its history — the kind of careful tenure that makes a 1925 farmhouse a 1925 farmhouse, instead of a 2024 renovation. — Eleanor Whitfield, Listing Broker

Location & neighborhood

218 River Road · Rhinebeck
Village of Rhinebeck · 1.6 mi Rhinecliff Amtrak · 2.1 mi Bard College · 7.4 mi Northern Dutchess Hospital · 4.0 mi Rhinebeck Farmers Market · 1.7 mi Mid-Hudson Bridge · 18 mi Hudson, NY · 22 mi Beacon Metro-North · 38 mi

River Road runs north out of Rhinebeck village along the eastern bluff of the Hudson, past a sequence of old farms, a small Episcopal church, and a stretch of conservancy land that protects the river view in both directions. The property's frontage is set back roughly four hundred feet from the road behind a stone wall and the maple row; from the road, only the chimney is visible. The nearest neighbor is a quarter mile to the south, in a 1830s clapboard house that the family has lived in for four generations.

The village of Rhinebeck — a 25-minute walk down a quiet country lane that becomes a quiet village street — provides everything practical: a year-round farmers market, a grocery, a 1766 inn, three coffee places that take making coffee seriously, a hardware store that still cuts keys, and a public library that hosts a quietly excellent literary series. Bard College's calendar of music, theater, and lecture programming sits fifteen minutes north. The Rhinecliff Amtrak station is six minutes south and runs eight trains a day to and from Manhattan.
